doc_summary: The paper builds a black-box lie detector that asks fixed unrelated yes/no follow-up questions and trains a logistic regression on GPT-3.5 prompted lies, then tests out-of-distribution generalisation to other models, fine-tuned liars, sycophancy and realistic goal-directed role-play scenarios. It stresses ruling out spurious correlations, testing against more realistic threat models, and being candid about non-watertight evidence.

items.claim: In a setup, give the model a goal and an incentive to lie inside a realistic role-play scenario with no explicit instruction to lie, instead of directly telling it to lie, because spontaneous goal-directed behaviour is the more realistic threat model.
items.quote: A key concern is when an LLM instructed to achieve a goal uses lying as a strategy, without explicitly being instructed to lie. We study this threat model with 52 real-life role-playing scenarios that contain no instruction to lie but may have an incentive to lie

items.claim: prefers testing realistic, topic-specific or goal-directed behaviour over blanket instructed behaviour because the realistic threat does not look like the simple lab elicitation.
items.quote: The prompts used so far instruct the model to lie to whatever question is asked. However, a more realistic threat comes from LLMs lying only about specific topics, e.g. for spreading misinformation.

items.claim: In a setup, pair each incentivised scenario with a matched control version that removes the incentive, and keep only transcripts where the target behaviour unambiguously occurred, instead of relying on a single scenario because this isolates the behaviour from scenario features.
items.quote: Each scenario has a version in which there is an incentive to lie (e.g. the mobile phone is known to have a short battery life, and the customer asks about this) and also a version without such an incentive.

items.claim: Operationalise the behaviour with a clear definition (wrong answer plus the model demonstrably knows the truth) and a control dataset where deviation is unambiguous, so the behaviour is not confused with honest mistakes.
items.quote: This dataset serves as a control; any model answer deviating from this one is an unambiguous lie.

items.claim: Distrusts results that could be explained by prompt artefacts or spurious correlates, and requires out-of-distribution checks such as unprompted fine-tuned models to rule them out.
items.quote: This spurious correlation is ruled out because the detector generalises to fine-tuned, unprompted, LLMs.

items.claim: prefers frozen-weight out-of-distribution generalisation over in-distribution accuracy as convincing evidence because real deployments involve unknown models, topics, and elicitation methods.
items.quote: A useful lie detector needs to generalise across various settings (Sec. 2). Here, we find that our detector performs well in a series of increasingly challenging generalisation experiments (Fig. 2).

items.claim: Is candid that evidence is not watertight and that capable future models may behave differently, so claims are hedged accordingly.
items.quote: However, as we can’t get conclusive evidence about more capable liars that we don’t have access to, our method may still require adaptation for models exhibiting more specific lying behaviour.

items.claim: Treats surprising generalisation or failure as a finding to report and probe rather than explain away, flagging explicitly what is not understood.
items.quote: This was unexpected, and we do not fully understand why this is the case, leaving this question for future research.

items.claim: Stress-tests behaviour by building adversarial prompts and transcripts specifically to find false positives and negatives, rather than only reporting average performance.
items.quote: we manually designed many prompts and conversation transcripts to find false positive and negative lie detection results.

items.claim: Favours black-box methods that work with third-party-controlled models and limited API access, since real deployment rarely gives internal access.
items.quote: This approach doesn’t require access to the LLM’s activations, allowing for its deployment in real-world settings involving third-party controlled LLMs

items.claim: Names future work on non-QA dialogues, instrumental lies in text-based games, and lies arising from RL fine-tuning, noting these are untested.
items.quote: We only study question-answering tasks. Future work could cover non-QA dialogues or instrumental lies in text-based games (Pan et al., 2023; O’Gara, 2023).
